draft.title: The 1905 Revolution
card: In 1904 and 1905, Russia lost a war against Japan. The defeats, especially the fall of Port Arthur and the loss of the fleet at Tsushima, shamed the tsar's government and showed how weak it was.

On 22 January 1905 (Old Style), troops fired on a peaceful march of workers in St Petersburg. The workers, led by Father Gapon, had come to petition the tsar for better conditions. Many were killed or wounded. The day became known as Bloody Sunday.

Bloody Sunday weakened trust in the tsar as protector of his people. Strikes, peasant revolts and mutinies followed across the empire, including the mutiny on the battleship Potemkin. In October a general strike spread.

In the October Manifesto, Nicholas II promised civil freedoms and an elected Duma, a national parliament. The tsar then limited the Duma's power through the Fundamental Laws of 1906, which kept his control of ministers and the army.
draft.remember: Defeat and Bloody Sunday sparked unrest. The tsar offered a Duma, then limited it.

a.q: Why did Bloody Sunday help spark the unrest of 1905?
opts: Troops shot peaceful petitioners, which broke trust in the tsar
Workers learned that Japan had defeated the Russian fleet
The tsar refused to create an elected Duma for Russia
Peasants were angered when the army seized their land
a.why: The workers marched to ask the tsar for help, and troops shot them. This broke the belief that the tsar cared for his people, and strikes and revolts followed. The defeat by Japan was a separate cause and did not happen on that day.
a.clue: Think about who was marching and who fired on them.

b.q: After the October Manifesto of 1905, Nicholas II issued the Fundamental Laws of 1906. What did they show about the Duma?
opts: The tsar kept real power and limited what the Duma could do
The tsar handed control of the army to the Duma
The Duma gained the power to choose and dismiss ministers
The tsar abolished the Duma soon after it was created
b.why: The Duma was created, but the Fundamental Laws left the tsar in control of ministers and the army, so its power was limited. It was not abolished, so the option about abolition is wrong: it still met, with less power than many had hoped.
b.clue: The Duma existed, but who still controlled the ministers and the army?
